metaDescription: Summerfield, Noble County landowner dealing with a Dormant Mineral Act dispute? See how Ohio case law like Dodd v. Croskey applies before you sell or claim.
heroLead: Noble County has been the setting for some of the actual court cases that shaped how Ohio's Dormant Mineral Act works today, and Summerfield sits right in the middle of that legal geography.
intro: Summerfield is a small village in Noble County, deep in the Utica/Point Pleasant core. Noble County land has been the subject of real Dormant Mineral Act litigation over the past decade, as surface owners and mineral heirs sorted out who actually held rights to interests that had gone unused for decades before shale drilling made them valuable again.

If your family's mineral interest near Summerfield has an unclear or disputed history, understanding how Ohio courts have actually applied the DMA is more useful than general assumptions about what the law says.

sections.heading: Dodd v. Croskey and what it clarified
paragraphs: Dodd v. Croskey, decided by Ohio's Seventh District Court of Appeals in 2013, addressed how the 1989 version of the Dormant Mineral Act applied to a Guernsey County interest and helped establish that the statute's notice and preservation requirements had to be followed precisely for a claim of abandonment to succeed.

That case, along with several others out of eastern Ohio's Seventh District, built the body of precedent that the Ohio Supreme Court later relied on in Corban v. Chesapeake to clarify that the 2006 amended version governs going forward, not automatic reversion under the older law.

sections.heading: What this means for an interest near Summerfield
paragraphs: If someone has claimed your family's mineral interest near Summerfield is abandoned, the specific facts matter enormously: when was notice given, was it done correctly, had there been any qualifying use like production or a recorded lease in the prior 20 years. General assumptions about dormancy do not settle these questions; the recorded documents do.
We review the Noble County Recorder's records as part of any offer to confirm there is no unresolved dormancy claim or open notice period affecting your interest before we quote a price.

sections.heading: Selling a confirmed, clean interest
paragraphs: Once your ownership is confirmed and no dormancy issue is outstanding, pricing follows the same approach as any other Noble County core interest, weighing lease status, nearby production, and current activity.
If a dormancy dispute is active, we can still discuss your situation, but resolving the title question, sometimes with an attorney's help, typically needs to happen before a clean sale can close.

faqs.question: What was Dodd v. Croskey about, and why does it matter near Summerfield?
faqs.answer: It was an eastern Ohio Dormant Mineral Act case that helped clarify how strictly the statute's notice requirements had to be followed. It is part of the case law background relevant to any Noble County dormancy question.

faqs.question: Someone told me our family's mineral rights near Summerfield were abandoned decades ago. Is that automatic?
faqs.answer: No. Under current Ohio Supreme Court precedent, abandonment is not automatic; it requires the surface owner to follow the specific statutory notice process, and prior use can defeat the claim.

faqs.question: How do I check if a dormancy claim has been filed against my interest?
faqs.answer: The Noble County Recorder's office maintains records of any notices or affidavits filed. We check this as part of our standard title review before making an offer.
